title: Spelling rules
blurb: Use the five core spelling rules (ie/ei, silent e, final y, doubling and prefixes) to spot the one misspelled word in a set.
question: A clinic leaflet says, “Patients who are refered by a physician will recieve a noticeable discount.” Two words are misspelled. Which rules do they break, and how do you find errors like these quickly on the TEAS?

teach.body: Formally, standard spelling is the conventional form of a word as listed in a standard US dictionary. Plain English: most words follow a handful of rules about how letters behave when you add an ending or a beginning. The TEAS usually shows four words or one sentence and asks which word is spelled correctly or incorrectly. Each wrong choice breaks one rule, often by over-applying it. Learn the five rules and their exceptions, and the wrong spellings start to look wrong.

head: Rule
Correct
Common wrong form
rows: i before e, except after c
Silent e + vowel suffix: drop e
Consonant + y: change y to i
teach.caption: Every rule has exceptions. The exceptions are exactly what the TEAS likes to test.

teach.h: Adding a suffix: which rule applies?

root.label: How does the base word end?

children.label: Drop e before a vowel suffix
children.sub: Keep it before a consonant suffix

children.label: Double if the last syllable is stressed

teach.caption: Vowel + y keeps the y (played, enjoyment). Never double w, x or y (fixing, snowing).

teach.h: Silent e: vowel suffix vs consonant suffix
teach.caption: Soft c or g keeps its e before -able or -ous so it stays soft: noticeable, manageable, outrageous.

teach.body: Double the final consonant before a vowel suffix when the word ends consonant-vowel-consonant and the stressed syllable is the last one: run, running; begin, beginning; refer, referred; control, controlled. Do not double when the stress falls earlier: open, opened; benefit, benefited; travel, traveled; cancel, canceled. Watch words where the stress moves: refer becomes referred (stress stays on -fer) but reference (stress moves to ref-), so only one r.

teach.caption: Traveled and canceled are the preferred US spellings. Travelled and cancelled are British forms that Merriam-Webster also lists as variants, so a fair item will not hinge on them.

teach.h: ie or ei, and the endings that trip people up
head: Pattern
Words
rows: either, neither, weird, seize, height, foreign, science
supersede only; exceed, proceed, succeed; all others -cede
teach.caption: -ful has one l (spoonful). Full + y becomes fully; all + ready becomes already.

teach.body: Jasmine Ortiz, a nursing applicant, checks this line: “Patients who are refered by a physician will recieve a noticeable discount.” Refered: refer is stressed on -fer, so the r doubles: referred. Recieve: ei follows c, so receive. Noticeable looks odd but is correct, because the soft c keeps its e before -able. She fixes two words and leaves the tricky-looking one alone.

teach.h: Spot the misspelled word in 4 moves
items: Find any ending added to a base word (-ed, -ing, -able, -ness, -ly).
Name the base word and apply the rule: silent e, final y or doubling.
Check any ie or ei against the rule and the short exception list.
Check prefixes (mis-, un-, dis-) kept every letter of the root, and reject UK forms such as colour or centre.

teach.text: The classic trap is over-applying a rule: “sieze” (seize is an exception), “noticable” (the soft c keeps its e), “truely” (true drops its e) and “occured” (occur is stressed on its last syllable, so the r doubles: occurred). A spelling that looks odd is not always wrong, and a UK-only spelling such as colour, centre or organise is wrong on a US exam.

items: i before e except after c or when it sounds like “ay”; learn the exceptions (either, weird, seize, height).
Silent e: drop before a vowel suffix, keep before a consonant suffix; soft c/g keeps e before -able/-ous.
Consonant + y: change to i, except before -ing; vowel + y keeps the y.
Double the final consonant only when the last syllable is stressed (occurred, but opened, traveled).
Prefixes never change the root (misspell, dissatisfied); only supersede ends in -sede.

summary: You can now apply the ie/ei, silent e, final y, doubling and prefix rules, including their exceptions and US spellings. You can also find the one misspelled word in a set or a sentence by checking each added ending against its rule.

A.q: Which of the following words is spelled correctly?
A.why: Ceiling follows the rule “e before i after c.”

whyNot.0: The ie in achieve does not follow c, so it is i before e: achieve.
whyNot.2: Weird is an exception to i before e; the correct spelling is weird.
whyNot.3: Seize is an exception to i before e; the correct spelling is seize.

A.q: Which word correctly adds a suffix to a base word that ends in silent e?
A.why: -ment begins with a consonant, so manage keeps its e: management.

whyNot.0: -ing begins with a vowel, so write drops its e: writing.
whyNot.1: -able begins with a vowel, so desire drops its e: desirable.
whyNot.2: The soft c in notice keeps its e before -able: noticeable.

A.q: Each word below adds a suffix to a base word that ends in y. Which one is spelled correctly?
A.why: Consonant + y keeps the y before -ing: carry becomes carrying.

whyNot.1: Consonant + y changes to i before -ness: happiness.
whyNot.2: Vowel + y keeps the y: stay becomes stayed.
whyNot.3: The y stays before -ing: study becomes studying.

B.q: Which word is spelled correctly in standard American English?
B.why: Refer is stressed on its last syllable, so the r doubles before -ed: referred.

whyNot.0: Begin is stressed on its last syllable, so the n doubles: beginning.
whyNot.1: Occur is stressed on its last syllable, so the r doubles: occurred.
whyNot.3: Visit is stressed on its first syllable, so the t does not double: visited.

B.q: Which word with a -ceed, -cede or -sede ending is spelled correctly?
B.why: Only three words end in -ceed: exceed, proceed and succeed.

whyNot.1: Precede is not one of the three -ceed words, so it ends in -cede.
whyNot.2: Succeed is one of the three -ceed words (exceed, proceed, succeed), so it ends in -ceed.
whyNot.3: Concede is not one of the three -ceed words, so it ends in -cede.

B.q: A student adds a prefix to a root word. Which result is spelled correctly?
B.why: A prefix never changes the root: dis + satisfied keeps both s's: dissatisfied.

whyNot.0: Mis + spelled keeps both s's: misspelled.
whyNot.1: Un + necessary keeps both n's: unnecessary.
whyNot.2: Dis + appointed has only one s, because appointed starts with a vowel: disappointed.

C.q: Which word in this sentence is misspelled? “The physician truely believed the noticeable improvement would continue until February.”
C.why: True is an exception that drops its e before -ly: truly.

whyNot.0: Believed follows i before e and drops the silent e before -ed, so it is correct.
whyNot.2: Noticeable is correct: the soft c keeps its e before -able.
whyNot.3: February is spelled correctly, including the first r that is often skipped in speech.

C.q: A patient leaflet for a US clinic must use standard American spelling. Which sentence is spelled correctly?
options: Our pediatric centre will analyze the results.
Our pediatric center will analyse the results.
Our pediatric center will analyze the results.
Our paediatric center will analyze the results.
C.why: US spelling uses center, analyze and pediatric.

whyNot.0: Centre is the British spelling; US English uses center.
whyNot.1: Analyse is the British spelling; US English uses analyze.
whyNot.3: Paediatric is the British spelling; US English uses pediatric.

C.q: Which pair of words is spelled correctly?
C.why: In preferred the stress stays on -fer, so the r doubles. In preference the stress moves to pref-, so it does not.

whyNot.0: Prefer is stressed on its last syllable, so the r doubles before -ed: preferred.
whyNot.1: The stress moves to the first syllable in preference, so there is one r: preference.
whyNot.2: Both words are wrong: preferred needs two r's and preference needs one.

reteach.title: Suffixes are guests at a door
reteach.question: Picture every suffix as a guest arriving at a word's front door. What does the word have to change to let each guest in?

blocks.body: A vowel guest (-ing, -ed, -able) cannot share the doorway with a silent e, so the e steps aside: hope, hoping. A consonant guest (-ful, -ment) fits fine, so the e stays: hopeful. A consonant + y word swaps its y for an i to greet most guests (happy, happiness) but not -ing, which would make two i's. And a short, stressed word like stop guards its door with an extra letter: stopped.

blocks.h: Checking one word, step by step

steps.label: Apply the rule
steps.sub: Not stressed last, so no doubling

blocks.text: Prefixes are guests at the front door, and they never change the word: mis + spell is misspell, with both s's.

explain.body: Write i before e (believe, field), except after c (receive, ceiling) or when the sound is “ay” (neighbor, weigh). Memorize the rule breakers: either, neither, weird, seize, leisure, height, foreign, science, species, ancient, protein.

test.q: Which word follows the ie/ei rule or its exceptions correctly?
test.why: Neighbor has the “ay” sound, so it takes ei.

whyNot.1: The ie does not follow c, so it is i before e: friend.
whyNot.2: Foreign is an exception that uses ei.
whyNot.3: The ie does not follow c, so it is i before e: believed.

explain.body: Silent e drops before a vowel suffix and stays before a consonant suffix, except after soft c or g before -able/-ous (courageous). Consonant + y changes to i (replies, beautiful) except before -ing; vowel + y keeps the y (enjoyment).

test.q: Which word keeps or drops its final letter correctly before the suffix?
test.why: The soft g in courage keeps its e before -ous: courageous.

whyNot.0: Argue is an exception that drops its e before -ment: argument.
whyNot.1: The soft c keeps its e before -able: noticeable.
whyNot.3: Consonant + y changes to i before -ment: accompaniment.

explain.body: Double the final consonant before a vowel suffix only when the word ends consonant-vowel-consonant and the last syllable is stressed (admitted, controlled). Do not double when the stress comes earlier (opened, benefited, traveled).

test.q: Which word applies the doubling rule correctly?
test.why: Control is stressed on its last syllable, so the l doubles: controlled.

whyNot.0: Consider is stressed on its second syllable, not its last, so the r does not double: considered.
whyNot.2: Open is stressed on the first syllable, so no doubling: opened.
whyNot.3: Admit is stressed on its last syllable, so the t doubles: admitted.

explain.body: Prefixes keep every letter of the root (misspell, unnecessary). The suffix -ful has one l (careful), but -ly is simply added to the adjective, so careful becomes carefully and final becomes finally. Words ending in -ic take -ally: basic becomes basically.

test.q: Which word ending in -ful, -fully or -ly is spelled correctly?
test.why: Careful + ly keeps both l's: carefully.

whyNot.1: The suffix -ful has one l: spoonful.
whyNot.2: Final + ly keeps both l's: finally.
